Pathology-01.question: ১) Which is excess production of scar tissue that is out of proportion to the wound?
Pathology-01.exp:
A keloid is an excessive overproduction of scar tissue (collagen) that extends beyond the original boundaries of the wound and is disproportionate to the injury. It results from abnormal wound healing with excessive fibroblast activity and collagen deposition.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Hypertrophic scar: Excess scar tissue formation, but it remains confined within the original wound margins and may regress over time.

  • Wound dehiscence: Separation or reopening of a wound due to failure of healing.

  • Naevus: A benign skin lesion (mole), not related to abnormal scar formation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Keloid Hypertrophic scar
Growth beyond wound margin Yes No
Collagen deposition Excessive Excessive
Regression Rare Common
Recurrence High Lower

Exam Pearl:
Keloid = Scar tissue growing beyond the original wound boundary due to excessive collagen deposition.

Pathology-01.question: ২) Chronic non lethal irritation results in
৩) Cumulative sub lethal injury over long life span causes
৪) The most common stimulus for hypertrophy of muscle is
Pathology-01.exp:
The most common stimulus for muscle hypertrophy is an increased workload. When a muscle is exposed to increased mechanical stress (e.g., resistance training), it adapts by increasing:

  • Cell size

  • Number of contractile proteins (actin and myosin)

  • Myofibril content

This results in enlargement of individual muscle fibers.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Decreased workload: Causes atrophy (reduction in muscle size).

  • Change in tissue type: Causes metaplasia, not hypertrophy.

  • Unexpected tissue death: Causes necrosis, not hypertrophy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Adaptation Stimulus
Hypertrophy Increased workload → ↑ cell size
Atrophy Decreased workload → ↓ cell size
Hyperplasia Increased cell number
Metaplasia Change from one mature cell type to another

Exam Pearl:
Muscle hypertrophy occurs mainly due to increased workload (mechanical stress), causing enlargement of existing muscle fibers.

Pathology-01.question: ৫) Key mediator of swelling in acute inflammation
Pathology-01.exp:
The key mediator responsible for swelling (edema) in acute inflammation is Histamine. Histamine is released mainly from mast cells and causes:

  • Vasodilation

  • Increased vascular permeability by causing endothelial cell contraction in post-capillary venules

  • Leakage of fluid and plasma proteins → swelling (edema)

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Bradykinin: Causes pain and increased vascular permeability, but it is not the principal mediator of acute inflammatory swelling.

  • Prostaglandin: Causes pain and fever; contributes to vasodilation.

  • Prostacyclin (PGI₂): Causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation; not the key mediator of swelling.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Mediator Main effect
Histamine Vasodilation + vascular permeability ↑ → edema
Bradykinin Pain + vascular permeability
Prostaglandins (PGE₂) Fever + pain
Leukotrienes Increased permeability, chemotaxis

Exam Pearl:
Acute inflammation edema = Histamine-mediated increased vascular permeability from mast cells.

Pathology-01.question: ৬) Pathological hypertrophy occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
Pathological hypertrophy occurs due to abnormal stress or increased workload on cells. The classic example is myocardial hypertrophy, which occurs in conditions like:

  • Hypertension → left ventricular hypertrophy

  • Aortic stenosis → pressure overload hypertrophy

Cardiac myocytes cannot significantly increase in number, so they adapt by increasing cell size and contractile protein content.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Uterus: Physiological hypertrophy during pregnancy due to hormonal stimulation (estrogen).

  • Breast: Physiological enlargement during puberty and pregnancy.

  • Skeletal muscle: Physiological hypertrophy due to exercise or increased workload.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypertrophy = increase in cell size.

  • Physiological hypertrophy: Uterus in pregnancy, skeletal muscle in exercise.

  • Pathological hypertrophy: Myocardium in hypertension and valvular heart disease.

Exam Pearl:
Myocardial hypertrophy due to chronic pressure overload is the classic example of pathological hypertrophy.

Pathology-01.question: ৭) Cancers grows by all of the followings except
Pathology-01.exp:
Malignant tumors grow by infiltration, invasion, and destruction of surrounding tissues. These properties allow cancer cells to spread locally and damage normal structures.

  • Infiltration: Cancer cells spread into surrounding tissues.

  • Invasion: Penetration through basement membrane and extracellular matrix.

  • Destruction: Malignant cells destroy normal tissues.

Cohesion is not a mechanism of cancer growth. In fact, loss of cellular cohesion (e.g., reduced E-cadherin expression) promotes invasion and metastasis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Infiltration: A feature of malignant tumor growth.

  • Invasion: A defining feature of cancer.

  • Destruction: Cancer causes tissue destruction by uncontrolled growth.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Benign tumor: Expansile growth, well-circumscribed, pushes surrounding tissue.

  • Malignant tumor: Invasion + infiltration + destruction + metastasis.

  • Loss of cohesion → increased metastatic potential.

Exam Pearl:
Cancer spreads by invasion and infiltration; loss of cohesion helps malignant cells invade.

Pathology-01.question: ৮) Cell number is increased in
Pathology-01.exp:
Hyperplasia is an adaptive cellular response characterized by an increase in the number of cells due to increased cell proliferation.

Examples:

  • Physiological hyperplasia: Enlargement of breast glandular tissue during puberty and pregnancy.

  • Pathological hyperplasia: Endometrial hyperplasia due to excess estrogen.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Hypertrophy: Increase in cell size, not cell number (e.g., myocardial hypertrophy).

  • Atrophy: Decrease in cell size and sometimes cell number.

  • Metaplasia: Replacement of one mature cell type by another mature cell type.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyperplasia = ↑ number of cells

  • Hypertrophy = ↑ size of cells

  • Atrophy = ↓ size of cells

  • Metaplasia = change of one differentiated cell type into another

Exam Pearl:
"Hyperplasia = more cells; Hypertrophy = bigger cells."

Pathology-01.question: ৯) Fatty change of the liver occurs in all of the following except -
Pathology-01.exp:
Fatty change (steatosis) of the liver occurs due to abnormal accumulation of triglycerides in hepatocytes. Common causes include:

  • Starvation (mobilization of fatty acids to the liver)

  • Protein-energy malnutrition (↓ apoprotein synthesis → impaired fat export)

  • Obesity (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)

Hemochromatosis, however, causes iron accumulation in the liver (hemosiderosis) leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis, not fatty change.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Starvation: Causes fatty liver due to increased fatty acid delivery to the liver.

  • Protein-energy malnutrition: Causes fatty liver due to defective lipoprotein synthesis.

  • Obesity: Common cause of fatty liver (NAFLD).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fatty change = Triglyceride accumulation in cells.

  • Causes of fatty liver: Alcohol, obesity, diabetes mellitus, starvation, protein malnutrition, toxins.

  • Hemochromatosis → Iron deposition → Bronze diabetes + Cirrhosis.

Exam Pearl:
Fatty liver = excess triglyceride; Hemochromatosis = excess iron (not fat).

Pathology-01.question: ১০) Which one is decreased in atrophy
Pathology-01.exp:
Atrophy is a decrease in the size of an organ or tissue due to reduction in:

  • Cell size (main mechanism)

  • Cell number (may occur due to apoptosis)

Therefore, both cell size and cell number can decrease in atrophy.

Examples:

  • Disuse atrophy of skeletal muscle → ↓ muscle fiber size

  • Brain atrophy → loss of neurons and reduced cell size

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Cell size: Decreased in atrophy, but not the only change.

  • Cell number: May decrease, but the major feature is reduced cell size.

  • None: Incorrect because atrophy involves reduction in cellular components.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Atrophy = ↓ organ size due to ↓ cell size ± ↓ cell number

  • Hypertrophy = ↑ cell size

  • Hyperplasia = ↑ cell number

  • Metaplasia = change of one mature cell type into another

Exam Pearl:
Atrophy mainly causes decreased cell size, but cell number may also decrease → Best answer: Both.

Pathology-01.question: ১১) Which one is age related atrophy?
Pathology-01.exp:
Senile atrophy is the age-related atrophy that occurs due to the natural aging process. It is caused by gradual loss of cells, reduced metabolic activity, and decreased regenerative capacity with advancing age.

Examples:

  • Brain atrophy in old age

  • Thinning of tissues due to aging

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Pressure atrophy: Occurs due to prolonged pressure causing tissue compression (e.g., pressure on bones by tumors).

  • Denervation atrophy: Occurs due to loss of nerve supply (e.g., muscle wasting after nerve injury).

  • Disuse atrophy: Occurs due to reduced functional activity (e.g., immobilized limb).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Senile atrophy = Age-related atrophy

  • Denervation atrophy = Loss of nerve supply

  • Disuse atrophy = Reduced workload/activity

  • Pressure atrophy = Chronic pressure effect

Exam Pearl:
Age-related reduction in tissue size and function = Senile atrophy.

Pathology-01.question: ১২) Which one is double edged sword?
Pathology-01.exp:
Metaplasia is called a “double-edged sword” because it is a protective adaptive response but may also increase the risk of malignancy if the persistent stimulus continues.

  • It is beneficial because one mature cell type is replaced by another type that can better tolerate stress.

  • However, prolonged metaplastic changes may progress to dysplasia and cancer.

Example:

  • Smoking → Squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium → Dysplasia → Bronchogenic carcinoma

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Atrophy: Decrease in cell size/number; not classically called a double-edged sword.

  • Hypertrophy: Increase in cell size; may be physiological or pathological but not termed double-edged sword.

  • Hyperplasia: Increase in cell number; can be pathological but the classic double-edged adaptation is metaplasia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Metaplasia = reversible adaptive change

  • Benefit: Protects against chronic stress

  • Risk: May progress → Dysplasia → Malignancy

  • Common example: Bronchial squamous metaplasia in smokers

Exam Pearl:
Metaplasia is a double-edged sword because it is protective initially but may predispose to cancer.

Pathology-01.question: ১৩) Metaplasia from squamous to columnar type may also occur in
Pathology-01.exp:
Barrett oesophagus is a classic example of metaplasia from squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium.

  • Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causes repeated injury to the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus.

  • The body adapts by replacing it with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells.

  • This metaplasia increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Aphthous ulcer: Causes mucosal ulceration; not a squamous-to-columnar metaplasia.

  • MALToma: A lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; not related to epithelial metaplasia.

  • Oesophageal varices: Dilated veins due to portal hypertension; no metaplastic change.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Barrett oesophagus: Squamous epithelium → Columnar epithelium

  • Cause: Chronic GERD

  • Complication: Esophageal adenocarcinoma

  • Another common metaplasia: Bronchial columnar epithelium → squamous epithelium in smokers

Exam Pearl:
Barrett oesophagus = intestinal columnar metaplasia of lower esophagus due to chronic acid reflux.

Pathology-01.question: ১৪) Abundant tissue stem cells are required in
১৫) Ischemic necrosis of brain indicates which type of necrosis?
Pathology-01.exp:
Ischemic necrosis of the brain produces liquefactive necrosis because brain tissue contains abundant lipids and hydrolytic enzymes with relatively few structural proteins. After ischemia, enzymatic digestion of dead cells occurs, resulting in a soft, liquid cavity (cyst formation).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Coagulative necrosis: Typical of ischemia in most solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen), but brain is the exception.

  • Caseous necrosis: Seen in tuberculosis and some fungal infections.

  • Fibrinoid necrosis: Occurs mainly in blood vessel walls during immune-mediated vascular injury.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Brain infarction → Liquefactive necrosis

  • Heart infarction → Coagulative necrosis

  • Tuberculosis → Caseous necrosis

  • Vessel wall immune injury → Fibrinoid necrosis

Exam Pearl:
Ischemia causes coagulative necrosis in most organs, but the brain shows liquefactive necrosis.

Pathology-01.question: ১৬) Enzymatic fat necrosis occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
Enzymatic fat necrosis occurs classically in acute pancreatitis. Pancreatic enzymes, especially lipase, leak into surrounding fat tissue and break down triglycerides into fatty acids. These fatty acids combine with calcium to form calcium soaps (saponification), producing chalky white deposits.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Breast: Can show traumatic fat necrosis, not enzymatic fat necrosis.

  • Uterus: Not a typical site of fat necrosis.

  • Kidney: Ischemic injury causes coagulative necrosis, not fat necrosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enzymatic fat necrosis → Acute pancreatitis

  • Enzyme involved → Lipase

  • Mechanism → Fat breakdown → Fatty acids + Calcium → Saponification

  • Breast fat necrosis → Trauma

Exam Pearl:
Pancreatitis causes enzymatic fat necrosis due to leakage of pancreatic lipase.

Pathology-01.question: ১৭) Not true about necrosis
১৮) Morphologic alterations in reversible cell injury excludes
১৯) Hydroxyl radical is inactivated by
Pathology-01.exp:
Hydroxyl radical (•OH) is one of the most reactive reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is detoxified mainly by antioxidant enzymes such as peroxiredoxins, which reduce reactive peroxides and protect cells from oxidative damage.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • SOD (Superoxide dismutase): Converts superoxide radical (O₂•⁻) into hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂); it does not directly inactivate hydroxyl radicals.

  • Glutathione peroxidase: Removes hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides using glutathione; not the main enzyme for hydroxyl radicals.

  • Caspases: Enzymes involved in apoptosis, not ROS detoxification.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • SOD: Superoxide (O₂•⁻) → H₂O₂

  • Catalase: H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂

  • Glutathione peroxidase: H₂O₂ + lipid peroxides → harmless products

  • Peroxiredoxins: Detoxify peroxides and protect against oxidative stress

Exam Pearl:
SOD handles superoxide, catalase/GPx handle hydrogen peroxide, while peroxiredoxins are important antioxidants against reactive peroxide species.

Pathology-01.question: ২০) Which free radical acts close to the site of production?
Pathology-01.exp:
The hydroxyl radical (•OH) is the most reactive and damaging free radical. Due to its extremely short half-life and high reactivity, it acts very close to the site where it is produced and causes immediate damage to nearby molecules such as:

  • DNA

  • Proteins

  • Lipid membranes

Hydroxyl radicals are mainly generated through the Fenton reaction involving hydrogen peroxide and iron.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Superoxide (O₂•⁻): Less reactive and can diffuse farther; converted by SOD to hydrogen peroxide.

  • Nitrite: Not a primary free radical involved in this context.

  • Peroxide (H₂O₂): A reactive oxygen species but not a free radical; can diffuse across membranes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most reactive ROS: Hydroxyl radical (•OH)

  • Acts at site of production: Hydroxyl radical

  • Superoxide: First ROS formed in mitochondria

  • H₂O₂: Converted by catalase and glutathione peroxidase

Exam Pearl:
Hydroxyl radical is the most toxic ROS and damages cellular components at the site where it is generated.

Pathology-01.question: ২১) Characteristics of apoptosis excludes
Pathology-01.option4: Removal of dead cells by Phagocytosis

Pathology-01.question: ২২) Which resembles necrosis morphologically & apoptosis mechanistically?

২৬) Cellular swelling results from all of the following except
২৭) Criteria of acute inflammation
২৮) Molecules involved in septic shock
২৯) Source of histamine is all of the following except
৩০) Which metabolite of arachidonic acid vasodialator?
৩১) Recruitment of Neutrophil & monocytes is done by
৩২) Disinfect surgical site prior to surgery
৩৩) Mediators of fever excludes
৩৪) Procarcinogens excludes
Pathology-01.exp:
Procarcinogens are substances that require metabolic activation (usually by cytochrome P450 enzymes) to become active carcinogens.

Examples:

  • Benzanthracene (Benzanthene) → Procarcinogen (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon)

  • Cycasin → Procarcinogen (found in cycad plants)

  • Benzidine → Procarcinogen (aromatic amine associated with bladder cancer)

Chlorambucil is an alkylating chemotherapeutic drug that acts as a direct-acting carcinogen/mutagen, not a classic procarcinogen.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Benzanthene: Requires metabolic activation → procarcinogen.

  • Cycasin: Requires activation to carcinogenic metabolites.

  • Benzidine: Requires metabolism and is linked with bladder carcinoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Procarcinogens: Need metabolic activation

    • Polycyclic hydrocarbons (benzopyrene/benzanthracene)

    • Aromatic amines (benzidine)

    • Natural compounds (cycasin)

  • Direct-acting carcinogens: Act without activation

    • Alkylating agents (e.g., chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide metabolites)

Exam Pearl:
Benzidine, cycasin, and benzanthracene are procarcinogens; chlorambucil is a direct-acting alkylating carcinogen.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৫) Bradykinin is a mediator of
৩৬) TNM staging of a malignant tumour -
Pathology-01.option3: Takes account of the secondary tumour size
Pathology-01.option4: Is not important for treatment planning
Pathology-01.exp:
TNM staging is a system used to describe the extent of malignant tumors:

  • T (Tumour): Size and extent of the primary tumour

  • N (Nodes): Regional lymph node involvement

  • M (Metastasis): Presence of distant metastasis (secondary tumour spread)

Therefore, TNM staging takes into account secondary tumour (metastatic) involvement, especially under the M category.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Only a clinical assessment: TNM can be assessed clinically (cTNM) and after surgery by histopathology (pTNM).

  • Cannot be done after surgery: Postoperative pathological staging is commonly performed.

  • Is not important for treatment planning: TNM staging is essential for prognosis and selecting treatment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • T = Primary tumour size/extent

  • N = Lymph node involvement

  • M = Distant metastasis

  • cTNM = Clinical staging

  • pTNM = Pathological staging after surgery

Exam Pearl:
TNM staging guides treatment decisions and prognosis; it includes primary tumour, nodes, and distant metastasi

Pathology-01.question: ৩৭) Gumma is found in
৩৮) Which one is malignant tumour?
৩৯) Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign tumor of
৪০) Criteria of malignant tumour excludes
৪১) MALT lymphoma is associated with
৪২) CA 15-3 is related to carcinoma of
৪৩) Which type of tumour mainly follows heamtogenous spread?
Pathology-01.exp:
Sarcomas mainly spread through the hematogenous route (blood vessels).

  • Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal/connective tissues (bone, muscle, fat, cartilage).

  • They commonly metastasize to the lungs via the bloodstream.

Examples:

  • Osteosarcoma → Lung metastasis

  • Soft tissue sarcoma → Hematogenous spread

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Carcinoma: Usually spreads through lymphatic vessels first (lymph node metastasis), although hematogenous spread can occur later.

  • Adenoma: Benign tumour; does not metastasize.

  • Fibroma: Benign tumour; does not metastasize.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Tumour type Main spread route
Carcinoma Lymphatic spread
Sarcoma Hematogenous spread
Melanoma Both lymphatic and hematogenous

Exam Pearl:
Sarcoma → Blood vessels → Lung metastasis is the classic pattern.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৪) Oncogenic microbes excludes
Pathology-01.exp:
Oncogenic microbes are infectious agents that can contribute to the development of cancer.

Important oncogenic viruses include:

  • HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

  • HPV (especially high-risk types 16, 18) → Cervical cancer and other anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, some Hodgkin lymphomas

VZV (Varicella-zoster virus) is not considered an oncogenic virus.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • HTLV-1: Associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

  • HPV: Major cause of cervical carcinoma.

  • EBV: Associated with multiple malignancies.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HPV → Cervical cancer

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma

  • HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

  • HBV/HCV → Hepatocellular carcinoma

  • HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma

Exam Pearl:
VZV is a herpesvirus but not an oncogenic virus.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৫) Grading of cancer is based on
Pathology-01.exp:
Grading of cancer refers to the assessment of how closely tumour cells resemble their normal tissue of origin (degree of differentiation).

  • Well-differentiated tumours resemble normal cells and are usually lower grade.

  • Poorly differentiated/anaplastic tumours have abnormal morphology and are usually higher grade with more aggressive behaviour.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Tumour size: Part of staging (T in TNM), not grading.

  • Nodal involvement: Part of staging (N in TNM).

  • Metastasis: Part of staging (M in TNM).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Based on
Grading Differentiation of tumour cells
Staging Tumour size + lymph nodes + metastasis (TNM)

Exam Pearl:
Grade = differentiation; Stage = extent of spread (TNM).

Pathology-01.question: ৪৬) Temperature for autoclaving
Pathology-01.exp:
Autoclaving is a method of sterilization that uses moist heat under pressure.

Standard autoclave condition:

  • Temperature: 121°C

  • Pressure: 15 psi (above atmospheric pressure)

  • Time: 15–20 minutes

This condition effectively kills:

  • Bacteria

  • Viruses

  • Fungi

  • Bacterial spores (highly resistant forms)

Why other options are incorrect:

  • 99°C: Below sterilization temperature; cannot reliably destroy spores.

  • 101°C: Around boiling point; not sufficient for sterilization.

  • 110°C: May not reliably kill all spores.

  • 121°C: ✅ Standard autoclave temperature.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Autoclave: 121°C, 15 psi, 15–20 min

  • Hot air oven: 160–170°C (dry heat)

  • Pasteurization: 63°C for 30 min or 72°C for 15 sec

Exam Pearl:
Autoclave = Moist heat sterilization at 121°C under 15 psi pressur

Pathology-01.question: ৪৭) IV solutions are sterilized by
৪৮) Which one is the hallmark of malignancy?
Pathology-01.exp:
Anaplasia is considered the hallmark of malignancy and refers to the lack of differentiation of tumour cells, meaning they lose their normal structural and functional characteristics.

Features of anaplasia:

  • Pleomorphism (variation in cell size and shape)

  • Hyperchromatic nuclei

  • Increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio

  • Abnormal mitotic figures

  • Loss of cellular differentiation

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Rapid growth:May occur in malignant tumours but is not the defining hallmark.

  • Metastasis:  A major feature of malignancy, but not all malignant tumours metastasize.

  • Local invasion: Important feature of malignancy, but anaplasia is the classic pathological hallmark.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Anaplasia = hallmark of malignancy

  • Metastasis = most reliable evidence of malignancy

  • Benign tumours → Well differentiated, cohesive, non-invasive

  • Malignant tumours → Anaplastic, invasive, metastatic

Exam Pearl:
Anaplasia is the pathological hallmark of malignancy; metastasis is the strongest evidence of malignant behaviour.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৯) Hypertrophy of an organ-
Pathology-01.option1: Means increased size due to increased number of cells
Pathology-01.option3: Is not seen where permanent cells make up the tissue
Pathology-01.exp:
Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells, resulting in enlargement of an organ. It occurs due to increased functional demand or hormonal stimulation.

In hypertrophied organs:

  • Cell size increases

  • Metabolic demand increases

  • Blood supply may become insufficient → relative ischemia can occur

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Increased size due to increased number of cells:  This describes hyperplasia, not hypertrophy.

  • Always a pathological process:  Hypertrophy can be physiological (e.g., skeletal muscle with exercise, pregnancy uterus).

  • Not seen where permanent cells make up the tissue:  Hypertrophy commonly occurs in tissues with permanent cells, e.g., cardiac muscle.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hypertrophy = ↑ cell size

    • Example: Left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension

  • Hyperplasia = ↑ cell number

    • Example: Endometrial hyperplasia

  • Permanent cells (e.g., cardiac myocytes) adapt mainly by hypertrophy

Exam Pearl:
Hypertrophy increases organ size by enlarging existing cells and may lead to ischemia due to increased demand.

Pathology-01.question: ৫০) Morphologic features of chronic inflammation are all of the following except -
Pathology-01.exp:
The main morphologic features of chronic inflammation are:

  1. Infiltration with mononuclear cells

    • Macrophages

    • Lymphocytes

    • Plasma cells

  2. Tissue destruction

  3. Repair with fibrosis (angiogenesis + collagen deposition)

Presence of exudates is mainly a feature of acute inflammation, where increased vascular permeability causes protein-rich fluid leakage.

Why other options are correct:

  • Infiltration with macrophages: ✅ Hallmark of chronic inflammation.

  • Fibrosis: ✅ Due to chronic tissue injury and repair.

  • Plasma cell infiltration: ✅ Common in chronic inflammatory conditions.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Acute inflammation Chronic inflammation
Neutrophils Macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells
Exudate formation Fibrosis
Rapid onset Prolonged duration
Edema prominent Tissue destruction + repair

Exam Pearl:
Chronic inflammation = macrophages + lymphocytes + plasma cells + fibrosis; exudate is mainly acute inflammation.
